content.p: For years Italian police described Salvatore Miceli of Salemi, a hill town in the province of Trapani, as the man who connected the Sicilian Mafia to the cocaine of South America. Prosecutors said he worked as a middleman between Cosa Nostra, the Calabrian 'Ndrangheta and the Colombian cartels, and the press nicknamed him the Mafia's "foreign minister". He was convicted in 2007 at Locri while he was still on the run, was seized in a Caracas hotel in June 2009, and was sentenced again in Palermo in March 2018 to 16 years for a later drug-trafficking case.
Much of the public record on him consists of police testimony, wiretaps and press reports of trials, and the reports do not always agree on dates.
content.h2: A Salemi family and an early record
content.p: According to Italian prosecutors quoted by the Associated Press, Miceli followed in the footsteps of his grandfather, the local Mafia boss Salvatore Zizzo. The same report said he was allegedly involved in the 1970s in a series of ransom kidnappings that helped finance drug-trafficking clans in nearby Trapani. In the early 1990s he faced drug and Mafia charges, but he was released pending trial, and he went on the run after being convicted in 2001.

That chronology is not shared by every account. The BBC and Reuters both wrote that he had been a fugitive since 2001. LiveSicilia, writing years later, placed his flight to Venezuela between 2003 and 2009. A newspaper report from June 2004 already listed him, aged 58, among the suspects who had escaped capture, describing him as considered chiefly responsible for large cocaine shipments.

The case that made his name began in the spring of 2003. On 30 May 2003 the State Police announced a dawn operation by officers from Trapani and Palermo working with the Guardia di Finanza. It followed a two-year investigation into links between the Mafia of Mazara del Vallo and 'Ndrangheta families of the Calabrian coast, and the police said the two groups had formed a consortium to bring in cocaine directly from Colombia. The announcement identified Miceli as a leading figure of the Salemi Mafia family who had been put in charge of the drug traffic by Cosa Nostra's leadership. Officers reported finding 220 kilograms of cocaine and a country house where, they said, he stored, processed and sold the drug.

A Gazzetta del Sud report a year later gave 31 May 2003 as the start of the operation, which it said led to the arrest of 20 of 30 suspects. It also described a 220-kilogram cocaine shipment, hidden in a container sent from South America, which investigators attributed to an order placed by Miceli and the Agate family of Mazara del Vallo with a Calabrian clan and the broker Roberto Pannunzi; the paper did not say whether this was the same 220 kilograms the police announced. Paul Waridel, a Lugano defendant, was convicted in connection with that shipment and sentenced to 18 years, the heaviest sentence the canton had handed down, the paper said.

The case took its name from "Sergi", the name of a clan from Platì, spelled backwards. When the trial reached Locri, Police official Giovanni Leuci testified in October 2005 that wiretaps made by the Trapani and Palermo police in April and August 2003 and in February 2004 indicated that Miceli was the link between Cosa Nostra and 'Ndrangheta clans of Platì in a vast cocaine trade from Colombia and Venezuela, working through Roberto Pannunzi and his son Alessandro. Leuci said that one recording indicated Miceli had been given the task of organising the traffic by Giuseppe Lipari, a 70-year-old from Palermo whom police and Carabinieri regarded as extremely close to the long-hidden boss Bernardo Provenzano. According to the report, the first attempt to bring in several tonnes of cocaine dated from 2000, when a ship called the Mirage II sailed from Colombia for Italy and sank off the coast of Venezuela.

The Igres trial at Locri lasted more than two years, with many of the defendants on the run. On 29 June 2007 the court, presided over by Olga Tarzia, convicted four men and acquitted nine. Miceli received the heaviest sentence, 23 years in prison, followed by Vito Bigione with 15, Mariano Agate with 13 and Giovanni Fornabaio with 6. Miceli, Bigione and Agate were also to be placed under supervised release for at least three years after serving their sentences.

Prosecutor Nicola Gratteri had asked for 333 years in total against 12 of the 13 defendants. For the thirteenth, the fugitive Mafia leader Matteo Messina Denaro, he had himself asked for acquittal, and the court duly acquitted him. At the time of the verdict Miceli was 61 years old and still at large.

On 21 June 2009 Italian police and Interpol officers, working with Venezuelan police, arrested Miceli in the Venezuelan capital. The BBC reported that he had been under surveillance for three days before he was seized. He was 63 and ranked on Italy's roster of its thirty most dangerous men. Italy's interior minister called the arrest an "important operation", and the BBC quoted a police statement saying the investigation had "essentially confirmed Miceli's primary role in the drug trafficking sector and his ability to build a close network of relations with various trans-national organised crime groups". A former head of the parliamentary anti-mafia commission told Reuters the capture was "a big blow to the Cosa Nostra".

The arrest came in a run of successes against the Mafia. The BBC recalled the capture of Provenzano in 2006, of his reported heir Salvatore Lo Piccolo in 2007 and of the 'Ndrangheta boss Pasquale Condello in February 2008. When InSight Crime reported another Mafia arrest in Venezuela, it recalled Miceli's capture in 2009 and called Venezuela a known refuge for mafiosi. The Associated Press, quoted by CounterVortex, said he would be deported to Italy.

Several accounts place him close to the top of the organisation. ANSA described him in 2018 as the trusted drugs kingpin of Matteo Messina Denaro, and said he had been appointed by Provenzano to run the traffic between South America and Italy. LiveSicilia, in a report on a separate money-laundering inquiry in 2011, called him a firm point of reference for Messina Denaro, and said he was suspected of being behind the entry of three men from the province into a mixed Sicilian-Calabrian group hit by an arrest order from a Reggio Calabria judge. That inquiry concerned a certificate of deposit said to be worth 870 million dollars, and the paper presented the link to Miceli as an investigators' suggestion, not an established fact.

LiveSicilia also repeated a story it described as hearsay: after a cocaine shipment ordered by Giovanni Brusca failed to arrive, a death sentence was said to have hung over Miceli until Messina Denaro stopped it.

Miceli's time behind bars produced the evidence for his second case. In February 2013, during a prison visit at Civitavecchia, he was recorded giving instructions to his son Mario Fortunato, passing him a note meant for another man, Michele Decina. LiveSicilia reported that the Carabinieri's special operations unit in Palermo and the Trapani investigators used the recordings to follow a group they believed was planning cocaine imports from Colombia, and that investigations ran from 2011 to 2014. Miceli was heard complaining that Decina had put an associate in touch with a Colombian supplier without asking him first.

The investigators tied part of the case to Pannunzi, arrested in a Bogota shopping centre on 5 July 2013 and sent to Italy two days later, according to InSight Crime (other reports of the time differ by a day or so). Gratteri called Pannunzi "the biggest cocaine importer in the world" and said he was the only broker able to sell to both the 'Ndrangheta and Cosa Nostra. LiveSicilia reported that on 11 March 2014 a 320-kilogram cocaine shipment hidden in metal tubes, bound for northern Europe aboard a coal carrier, was seized at Santa Marta in Colombia. According to the Carabinieri, 20 kilograms of it were meant for the Sicilian group.

In 2016 a judge at the preliminary stage refused to order the arrest of the suspects, ruling that so much time had passed that there was no current need for detention, and that the alleged association was not proved. Miceli's son and Decina stayed free. The prosecutors appealed.

On 21 March 2018 the preliminary-hearing judge, Cesare Vincenti, convicted six men. Salvatore Miceli received 16 years, his son Mario Fortunato 14, Michele Decina and Michele and Gaetano Gregoli of Palermo 12 years each, and Emanuele Saglimbene 9 years and 4 months. Three defendants were acquitted, among them Pannunzi. Apart from Salvatore Miceli, all the convicted men remained free, under supervised release and a ban on leaving the country, because the 2016 ruling had found no present danger. The sentences were first instance only, and the sources do not report an appeal.

LiveSicilia reported that, once in prison, Miceli was suspected of trying to set up fresh trafficking with men close to the Morabito-Palamara-Bruzzaniti clan of Africo. ANSA added that he had spent eight years among Italy's 30 most dangerous fugitives.
